claim: Prion diseases are caused by PrPSc, a self-replicating pathologically misfolded protein that exerts toxicity predominantly in the brain.
source: Prion diseases are caused by PrPSc, a self-replicating pathologically misfolded protein that exerts toxicity predominantly in the brain.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established knowledge about prion diseases.

claim: Terminally diseased mice with severe neurological symptoms showed extensive alterations in astrocytes and microglia.
source: Terminally diseased mice with severe neurological symptoms showed extensive alterations in astrocytes and microglia.
evidence: This claim is supported by the ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript showing differential translation in these cell types.

claim: Only minor changes were detected in the translational profiles of neurons during prion disease.
source: Surprisingly, we detected only minor changes in the translational profiles of neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the ribosome profiling data showing few differentially translated genes in neuronal populations.

claim: Prion-induced alterations in glia overlapped with those identified in other neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Prion-induced alterations in glia overlapped with those identified in other neurodegenerative diseases, suggesting that similar events occur in a broad spectrum of pathologies.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published signatures from other neurodegenerative diseases mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Aberrant translation within glia may suffice to cause severe neurological symptoms and may be the primary driver of prion disease.
source: Our results suggest that aberrant translation within glia may suffice to cause severe neurological symptoms and may even be the primary driver of prion disease.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the finding of extensive glia changes but minimal neuronal changes in the presence of severe symptoms.

claim: Prions consist primarily of PrPSc, pathological aggregates of the cellular prion protein (PrPC).
source: Prions consist primarily of PrPSc, pathological aggregates of the cellular prion protein (PrPC) and can be highly infective.
evidence: This is established knowledge about prion composition cited from the literature (Scheckel and Aguzzi, 2018).

claim: All prion diseases show a similar disease progression characterized by pronounced vacuolation phenotype, activation of microglia and astrocytes, and ultimately neuronal loss.
source: While the cause of PrPC aggregation differs, all PrDs show a similar disease progression characterized by a pronounced vacuolation phenotype, activation of microglia and astrocytes, and ultimately neuronal loss.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about prion disease pathology.

claim: Mouse models of prion disease recapitulate most aspects of human disease including transcriptomic changes.
source: In particular, mouse models of PrD appear to recapitulate most aspects of the human disease including transcriptomic changes – a finding that sets them apart from other murine models of neurodegenerative disease (Burns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burns et al., 2015.

claim: Genes linked to neurodegeneration in humans are conspicuously downregulated in prion disease mice.
source: Importantly, PrDs share many hallmarks with other more common neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease, and genes linked to neurodegeneration in humans have been shown to be conspicuously downregulated in PrD mice (Burns et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burns et al., 2015.

claim: RiboTag mice expressing HA tagged ribosomes in a Cre recombinase-dependent manner have been used to profile multiple CNS cell populations without tissue manipulation procedures.
source: RiboTag (RT) mice expressing HA tagged ribosomes in a Cre recombinase-dependent manner (Sanz et al., 2009), have been used to profile multiple CNS cell populations without tissue manipulation procedures (Boisvert et al., 2018; Furlanis et al., 2019; Haimon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations describing the use of RiboTag mice.

claim: The CamKIIa promoter induced GFP expression in only a subset of NeuN+ neurons.
source: Co-staining with the neuronal marker NeuN, which is expressed in most neurons, confirmed that the CamKIIa promoter induced GFP expression in only a subset of NeuN+ neurons.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: GFP-expressing PV neurons were typically NeuN negative.
source: In contrast, GFP-expressing PV neurons were typically NeuN negative.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The GFP:Rpl10a mouse strain does not exhibit leaky constitutive GFP expression.
source: Importantly, the expression of GFP was strictly Cre-dependent (Figure 1b–c and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) indicating that the GFP:Rpl10a mouse strain does not exhibit leaky constitutive GFP expression.
evidence: This is supported by the absence of GFP signal in Cre-negative mice shown in Figure 1.

claim: The mGFAP line 77.6 expresses Cre almost exclusively in astrocytes.
source: The mGFAP line 77.6 utilized in this study performs better than other astrocytic Cre drivers and expresses Cre almost exclusively in astrocytes (Gregorian et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gregorian et al., 2009.

claim: The Cx3cr1CreER line displays Cre-induced rearrangements in microglia and neurons due to Cx3cr1 promoter activity during neuronal development.
source: Also, the microglia Cre driver line, Cx3cr1Cre has been shown to display Cre-induced rearrangements not only in microglia but also in neurons, most likely due to Cx3cr1 promoter activity during neuronal development (Haimon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haimon et al., 2018.

claim: Cx3cr1CreER mice express Cre in non-parenchymal macrophages corresponding to roughly ~1% of Cre-positive cells.
source: While these mice showed GFP expression in microglia and not in neurons (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1e), they have been reported to additionally express Cre in non-parenchymal macrophages (Goldmann et al., 2016), corresponding to roughly ~1% of Cre-positive cells in Cx3cr1CreER mice (Haimon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Goldmann et al., 2016 and Haimon et al., 2018.

claim: Glial GFP, IBA-1, and GFAP levels were markedly increased in terminal prion disease brains.
source: Consistently, glial GFP, IBA-1 (microglia marker) and GFAP (astrocyte marker) levels were markedly increased in terminal PrD brains.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: No clear difference in neuronal GFP, NeuN, CamKIIa or PV expression was observed between control and terminal prion disease brains.
source: In contrast, we did not observe a clear difference in neuronal GFP, NeuN, CamKIIa or PV expression (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: No or only a minor decrease in neuronal cell number was evident at the terminal prion disease stage in mice.
source: This is consistent with previous observations from our lab, where no or only a minor decrease in neuronal cell number was evident at the terminal PrD stage in mice.
evidence: This is based on previous observations from the authors' laboratory.

claim: The number of ribosome-protected fragments is linked to the number of ribosomes per transcript and therefore to the translation rate.
source: The number of RPFs is linked to the number of ribosomes per transcript and therefore to the translation rate.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about ribosome profiling methodology.

claim: Libraries typically obtained 5–10 million unique reads per library.
source: We typically obtained 5–10 million unique reads per library (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and Supplementary file 1), of which only a minority (≤10%) mapped to ribosomal RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Only a minority (≤10%) of aligned reads mapped to ribosomal RNA.
source: We typically obtained 5–10 million unique reads per library (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a and Supplementary file 1), of which only a minority (≤10%) mapped to ribosomal RNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Most aligned reads were coding sequence (CDS) reads.
source: Most aligned reads were coding sequence (CDS) reads (Figure 2b and Supplementary file 1), which is consistent with the ribosome occupancy of transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2b and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Libraries of all terminally diseased mice were non-distinguishable from other libraries despite the increase in glia cells at the terminal stage.
source: Importantly, despite the increase in glia cells at the terminal stage, the libraries of all terminally diseased mice (green data points in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1) were non-distinguishable from other libraries.
evidence: This is supported by quality control data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Principal-component analysis and hierarchical clustering revealed a segregation of different cell types.
source: A principal-component analysis (PCA) and hierarchical clustering based on Euclidean distances revealed a segregation of the different cell types as well as a similarity between the analyzed neuronal cell types (Figure 2c–d and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by PCA and clustering data shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: Cre-negative samples were most similar to GFAP samples.
source: With astrocytes being a highly abundant cell type in the CNS (Miller, 2018), it was not surprising that Cre-negative samples were most similar to GFAP samples (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by PCA data shown in Figure 2c and citation to Miller, 2018.

claim: The top 100 enriched genes in neurons, endothelial cells, oligodendrocytes, astrocytes and microglia showed the highest translation in the corresponding ribosome profiling dataset.
source: We defined the top 100 enriched genes in neurons (N), endothelial cells (EC), oligodendrocytes (OL), astrocytes (AS) and microglia (MG) based on RNA sequencing data generated from these cell populations (Zhang et al., 2014). These cell types were purified from P7 mouse brains via cell dissociation, immunopanning and FACS, and were analyzed via RNAseq. In contrast, our datasets were generated via ribosome profiling of flash-frozen brain regions from 13-week-old mice. Nonetheless, we observed that the top 100 enriched genes showed the highest translation in the corresponding RP dataset (Figure 3a and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published data from Zhang et al., 2014 shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Cell-type-specific markers showed the highest translation in the respective cell type.
source: We additionally assessed cell-type-specific markers, defined by single-cell sequencing of the visual cortex from 2-month-old mice (Hrvatin et al., 2018). As expected, marker genes for excitatory neurons, PV neurons, astrocytes and microglia showed the highest translation in the respective cell type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with published data from Hrvatin et al., 2018 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ribosome profiling predominantly profiled subsets of excitatory neurons (L23, L5_1 and L5_3) and microglia (Micro_1).
source: The comparison further revealed that we predominantly profiled subsets of excitatory neurons (L23, L5_1 and L5_3) and microglia (Micro_1).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with single-cell sequencing markers.

claim: Macrophage markers were highly translated in the Cx3cr1 ribosome profiling dataset.
source: Additionally, macrophage markers were highly translated in the Cx3cr1 RP dataset, confirming previous observations that a minor fraction of Cx3cr1CreER-positive cells are non-parenchymal macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of marker gene translation and confirms previous observations.

claim: A total of 2692 preferentially translated genes were identified, including 57 CamKIIa_CX, 50 CamKIIa_HC, 299 PV, 963 GFAP and 1323 Cx3Cr1 PTGs.
source: This yielded a total of 2692 PTGs, including 57 CamKIIa_CX, 50 CamKIIa_HC, 299 PV, 963 GFAP and 1323 Cx3Cr1 PTGs (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Ribosome profiling and RiboTag datasets of each cell type were overall highly correlated.
source: While RT and RP datasets of each cell type were overall highly correlated (Figure 3d), we also observed that a number of genes deviated from the linear regression line, including several PTGs (colored in Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Prion-induced changes only became evident at later disease time points.
source: Prion-induced changes only became evident at later disease time points, and except for few individual genes we could not detect any DTGs in any of the cell types at 2, 4, 8, and 16 weeks post prion inoculation (wpi).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis across time points shown in Figure 4a.

claim: A clear separation of control and prion disease samples was observed only at the terminal time point, most strikingly in GFAP and Cx3cr1+ cells.
source: A PCA revealed a clear separation of control and PrD samples only at the terminal time point, most strikingly in GFAP and Cx3cr1+ cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by PCA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both GFAP+ and Cx3cr1+ cells showed several translational changes at the pre-terminal stage, 24 weeks post inoculation.
source: Both of these cell types already showed several translational changes at the pre-terminal stage, 24 wpi.
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: There was a high overlap between the changes at 24 weeks post inoculation and terminal time points in GFAP+ and Cx3cr1+ cells, especially among upregulated genes.
source: Upon comparing prion-induced changes at the last two time points, we observed a correlation in both GFAP+ and Cx3cr1+ cells and a high overlap between the changes at the two time points, especially among upregulated genes (Figure 4b–c).
evidence: This is supported by comparison data shown in Figure 4b-c.

claim: Pronounced translational changes in astrocytes and microglia become evident 2 months before the terminal stage, long before any prion disease-related symptoms manifest.
source: This indicates that the pronounced translational changes in astrocytes and microglia become evident 2 months before the terminal stage, long before any PrD-related symptoms manifest.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of changes at 24 wpi relative to terminal disease.

claim: A1 signature genes increased with disease progression.
source: Not surprisingly, we found A1 signature genes to increase with disease progression (Figure 4d and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of A1 signature genes shown in Figure 4d.

claim: A2 signature genes increased with disease progression.
source: We also observed an increase in A2 signature genes, corresponding to neurotrophic factors (Liddelow et al., 2017; Zamanian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of A2 signature genes shown in Figure 4d and citations.

claim: Disease-associated microglia (DAM) genes increased during disease progression.
source: Consistent with our observations for A1 genes, disease-associated microglia (DAM) genes increased during disease progression.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of DAM signature genes shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Homeostatic microglia markers started to show a slight decrease at 24 weeks post inoculation, that was more pronounced at the terminal stage of the disease.
source: In contrast, homeostatic microglia markers started to show a slight decrease at 24 wpi, that was more pronounced at the terminal stage of the disease (Figure 4e and Supplementary file 8).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of homeostatic microglia genes shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The appearance of disease-associated microglia and the concomitant loss of homeostatic microglia are hallmarks of multiple neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Similar observations have been reported for multiple neurodegenerative diseases (Keren-Shaul et al., 2017), confirming that the appearance of DAMs and the concomitant loss of homeostatic microglia are hallmarks of multiple neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Keren-Shaul et al., 2017.

claim: Neuronal cell types displayed very few translational changes even at the terminal stage.
source: Surprisingly, neuronal cell types displayed very few translational changes even at the terminal stage (Figure 4a), and we observed only a low correlation of prion-induced changes at the last two time points (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Several genes that changed in neurons at 24 weeks post inoculation were enriched in either astrocytes and/or microglia, suggesting these changes might reflect glia contamination.
source: Several of the genes that changed in neurons at 24 wpi were enriched in either astrocytes and/or microglia and these changes might reflect a glia contamination.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of cell-type enrichment of changing genes.

claim: Sik1, Cyp2s1, and Oprm1 were highest expressed in neurons.
source: Yet Sik1 (changing in CamKIIa cortical neurons) and Cyp2s1 and Oprm1 (both changing in PV neurons) were highest expressed in neurons, and it is possible that even such few changes are sufficient to induce neuronal dysfunction and symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of gene expression patterns and represents speculation about functional consequences.

claim: Five genes showed an increase in translation in all analyzed cell types: Gfap, Serpina3n, Apod, Mt1, and Lgals3bp.
source: Yet, five genes showed an increase in translation in all analyzed cell types: Gfap, Serpina3n, Apod, Mt1, and Lgals3bp (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: All five genes that changed in all cell types are highly translated in astrocytes, microglia or both.
source: All five genes are highly translated in astrocytes, microglia or both (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and Supplementary file 9), indicating that the increase in neuronal translation of these common genes is likely a contamination and reflects the pronounced astro- and microgliosis at the terminal PrD stage.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of cell-type-specific translation patterns shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Pronounced regional differences in translation were detected within one and the same cell type.
source: Interestingly, we detected pronounced regional differences in translation within one and the same cell type.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of CamKIIa changes between cortex and hippocampus shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The CamKIIa changes between cortex and hippocampus did not correlate.
source: The CamKIIa changes between cortex and hippocampus did not correlate (Figure 5d) and, apart from the common genes discussed above, only one additional gene was shared between the CamKIIa datasets.
evidence: This is supported by comparison shown in Figure 5d.

claim: 170 genes changed in both glia cell types, with most of them (n = 153) changing in the same direction.
source: Yet, we also identified 170 genes that changed in both glia cell types, with most of them (n = 153) changing in the same direction.
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Immune response genes were enriched among genes that increased specifically in astrocytes, microglia, or in both cell types.
source: We found an enrichment of immune response genes among all three groups of genes and, among astrocyte-specific increasing genes, an enrichment of terms related to cell adhesion and extracellular matrix organization, indicating that these processes might be affected in astrocytes (Figure 5f and Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Many decreasing genes that are astrocyte-specific or shared have been linked to sterol and cholesterol biosynthesis.
source: In contrast, many decreasing genes that are astrocyte-specific (n = 184) or shared (n = 17) have been linked to sterol and cholesterol biosynthesis, respectively, whereas microglia-specific decreasing genes (n = 640) were enriched for neuronal terms including synaptic transmission (Figure 5f and Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Microglia-specific decreasing genes were enriched for neuronal terms including synaptic transmission.
source: In contrast, many decreasing genes that are astrocyte-specific (n = 184) or shared (n = 17) have been linked to sterol and cholesterol biosynthesis, respectively, whereas microglia-specific decreasing genes (n = 640) were enriched for neuronal terms including synaptic transmission (Figure 5f and Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Many microglia-specific decreasing genes were strongly enriched in neuronal cell types.
source: Indeed, we observed a negative correlation between the translational change in microglia and neuronal enrichment: many microglia-specific decreasing genes (colored in blue) were strongly enriched in neuronal cell types (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c: first three panels).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The decrease in neuronal-enriched genes specifically in microglia is likely an artefact and reflects a change in the composition of analyzed cell types, namely the increase in microglia relative to neurons.
source: The decrease in neuronal-enriched genes specifically in microglia is thus likely an artefact and reflects a change in the composition of analyzed cell types, namely the increase in microglia relative to neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between microglia changes and neuronal enrichment.

claim: The datasets correlated at the terminal stage between mRNA abundance and cell-type-specific translation.
source: While we did not observe a correlation between mRNA abundance and cell-type-specific translational changes at 8 wpi (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a), the datasets correlated at the terminal stage (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b), and many genes changed in both mRNA abundance and cell-type-specific translation (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with RNAseq data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Microglia preferentially translated genes showed a strong increase in the RNAseq dataset.
source: We previously reported that terminal mRNA abundance changes correspond to genes enriched in microglia and astrocytes. Consistently, we observed that microglia PTGs showed a strong increase in the RNAseq dataset (Figure 6b), and that more than a third of the genes changing in mRNA abundance are microglia PTGs (566 out of 1451), most of which specifically changed in the RNAseq dataset (Figure 6a, n = 411).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with RNAseq data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The RNAseq dataset showed the highest correlation with GFAP translational changes.
source: The RNAseq dataset showed the highest correlation with GFAP translational changes (Figure 6c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b), which is consistent with astrocytes being the most abundant cell type.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Many genes that increased in mRNA abundance were enriched in microglia and thus reflect microglia proliferation rather than an increase in microglia-gene expression on a cellular level.
source: Yet, many genes that increased in mRNA abundance were enriched in microglia (Figure 6d), and thus reflect microglia proliferation rather than an increase in microglia-gene expression on a cellular level.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of RNAseq and cell-type-specific translation data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: No change in cell-type-specific translation nor protein expression in whole brain extracts was observed for Glul.
source: While we observed no change in cell-type-specific translation nor protein expression in whole brain extracts for Glul, the protein expression and the translation in all assessed cell types strongly increased for Gfap (Figure 6e–f and Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by translation and western blot data shown in Figure 6e-f.

claim: The protein expression and the translation in all assessed cell types strongly increased for Gfap.
source: While we observed no change in cell-type-specific translation nor protein expression in whole brain extracts for Glul, the protein expression and the translation in all assessed cell types strongly increased for Gfap (Figure 6e–f and Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by translation and western blot data shown in Figure 6e-f.

claim: The number of astrocytes does not change during prion disease.
source: This indicates that the number of astrocytes does not change during PrD, yet specific genes such as Gfap are strongly upregulated in astrocytes during PrD progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Glul does not change while Gfap increases.

claim: An increase in both IBA1 and MMP9 protein expression was observed, whereas Aif1 translation did not change and Mmp9 translation even decreased, specifically in microglia.
source: In contrast, we observed an increase in both IBA1 and MMP9 protein expression, whereas Aif1 translation did not change and Mmp9 translation even decreased, specifically in microglia (Figure 6e–f and Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by translation and western blot data shown in Figure 6e-f.

claim: The increased microglia proliferation accounts for the increase in IBA1 protein levels and additionally masks the microglia-specific decrease in Mmp9 translation.
source: The increased microglia proliferation therefore not only accounts for the increase in IBA1 protein levels (no cell-type specific change in translation was detectable), but also additionally masks the microglia-specific decrease in Mmp9 translation.
evidence: This is inferred from the discrepancy between protein levels and cell-type-specific translation.

claim: No decrease in neuronal markers was observed in prion disease.
source: We additionally assessed NeuN expression in hippocampal and cortical lysates as well as PV expression in whole brain lysates but did not observe a decrease in neuronal markers in PrD (Figure 6g and Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Terminally sick prion disease mice show no or only little neuronal loss.
source: These results support our initial observation (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) that terminally diseased PrD mice showed no or only little neuronal loss and explain why neuronal enriched genes show no or only a minor decrease in the RNAseq dataset (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by western blot and immunohistochemistry data.

claim: GFP levels remained constant in GFAP Cre/Rpl10a:GFP mice.
source: GFP levels remained constant in GFAP Cre/Rpl10a:GFP mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2b), indicating that an increased GFAP promoter activity does not lead to additional Cre recombination events.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2b.

claim: GFP levels increased in Cx3cr1 Cre/Rpl10a:GFP mice, most likely reflecting the increase in microglia numbers.
source: In contrast, GFP levels increased in Cx3cr1 Cre/Rpl10a:GFP mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c), most likely reflecting the increase in microglia numbers.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c and represents inference about the cause.

claim: Cell-type-specific ribosome profiling identified ~1500 novel genes that showed prion disease-dependent translational changes, which were missed with more conventional approaches such as RNAseq of brain regions.
source: Collectively, our data highlights the importance of studying individual cell types, allowing us to identify ~1500 novel genes that showed PrD-dependent translational changes, which were missed with more conventional approaches such as RNAseq of brain regions.
evidence: This is supported by comparison between ribosome profiling and RNAseq datasets.

claim: The murine prion disease model assessed did not show a major decrease in neurons at the terminal stage.
source: The murine PrD model assessed here did not show a major decrease in neurons at the terminal stage.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry and western blot data.

claim: The difference in neuronal loss between mice and humans is likely to reflect a difference in the disease stage.
source: Compared to humans, whose lives can be somewhat prolonged due to medical interventions, mice must be euthanized at a relatively early endpoint, well ahead of terminal disease, in order to comply with animal-welfare regulations. While these rules may have some justification, they render it legally impossible to investigate the true endpoint of mouse prion models. Consequently, the difference in neuronal loss is likely to reflect a difference in the disease stage.
evidence: This is speculation based on the constraints of animal welfare regulations.

claim: It is possible that even few translational changes in neurons suffice to induce neurological dysfunction and symptoms.
source: It is possible that even few translational changes in neurons suffice to induce neurological dysfunction and symptoms.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional consequences of the observed changes.

claim: Neurological changes may be evoked by subtle differences affecting neuronal connectivity, which may be induced by the widespread glia alterations but may escape translational analyses.
source: Alternatively, neurological changes are evoked by subtle differences affecting neuronal connectivity, which may be induced by the widespread glia alterations described above but may escape translational analyses.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative mechanisms that could explain the symptoms.

claim: Mice overexpressing PrP show a protracted UPR activation leading to increased phosphorylation of PERK and eIF2α, a global decrease in translation, as well as increased ATF4/CHOP expression and apoptosis.
source: Translation of mRNA has previously been shown to be affected in a PrD mouse model which overexpresses PrP and are thus characterized by an accelerated PrD progression with pronounced loss of synapses and neurons (Moreno et al., 2012). These mice show a protracted UPR activation leading to increased phosphorylation of PERK and eIF2α, a global decrease in translation (including of Actb, Snap25, and Psd95), as well as increased ATF4/CHOP expression and apoptosis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Moreno et al., 2012.

claim: Neuronal overexpression of GADD34 globally decreased eIF2α phosphorylation in hippocampal extracts, rescued the reduced translation and neuronal loss, and increased survival.
source: While it remains unclear in which cell types these changes occur, neuronal overexpression of GADD34 globally decreased eIF2α phosphorylation in hippocampal extracts, rescued the reduced translation and neuronal loss, and increased survival.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work from the same group.

claim: Astrocytic overexpression of GADD34 was neuroprotective and increased survival.
source: More recently, the same group could show that also astrocytic overexpression of GADD34 was neuroprotective and increased survival (Smith et al., 2020), highlighting the importance of astrocytes in neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith et al., 2020.

claim: In the prion disease mouse model used in this study, none of the analyzed cell types showed a differential translation of Actb, Snap25, Psd95 (Dlg4), or Chop.
source: Interestingly, in our PrD mouse model none of the analyzed cell types showed a differential translation of Actb, Snap25, Psd95 (Dlg4), or Chop and only microglia showed an increased translation of Atf4.
evidence: This is supported by the ribosome profiling data from this study.

claim: Only microglia showed an increased translation of Atf4.
source: Interestingly, in our PrD mouse model none of the analyzed cell types showed a differential translation of Actb, Snap25, Psd95 (Dlg4), or Chop and only microglia showed an increased translation of Atf4.
evidence: This is supported by the ribosome profiling data from this study.

claim: An increase in Gadd34 translation was observed specifically in astrocytes.
source: In addition, while Moreno et al. did not observe an increased expression of GADD34 in hippocampal extracts, we observed an increase in Gadd34 translation specifically in astrocytes, presumably leading to a reduced UPR.
evidence: This is supported by the ribosome profiling data from this study.

claim: A reduced UPR activation in the mouse model used in this study might contribute to a less pronounced neurodegeneration.
source: Considering the differences in UPR marker expression and neuronal loss between the different PrD mouse models, it is plausible that a reduced UPR activation in our mouse model might contribute to a less pronounced neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with other models.

claim: Previously identified glia signatures increased in the dataset, including disease associated microglia (DAM) genes as well as neurotoxic (A1) astrocyte genes.
source: Previously identified glia signatures increased in our dataset, including disease associated microglia (DAM) genes as well as neurotoxic (A1) astrocyte genes.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of known signatures in the ribosome profiling data.

claim: Homeostatic microglia genes decreased during prion disease progression.
source: In contrast, homeostatic microglia genes decreased during PrD progression.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of homeostatic microglia signatures in the ribosome profiling data.

claim: A1-astrocyte ablation in prion-inoculated mice accelerated disease progression, indicating that A1 astrocytes in prion disease could be neuroprotective.
source: Yet, while preventing A1 formation after acute CNS injury reduced the loss of axotomized neurons (Liddelow et al., 2017), A1-astrocyte ablation in prion-inoculated mice accelerated disease progression (Hartmann et al., 2019), indicates that A1 astrocytes in PrD could be neuroprotective.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liddelow et al., 2017 and Hartmann et al., 2019.

claim: Astrocytes might play a central role in limiting prion toxicity.
source: Combined with our observations that neurotrophic (A2) astrocyte genes and Gadd34 increase in astrocytes, these results suggest that astrocytes might play a central role in limiting prion toxicity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of data showing A2 gene increases and Gadd34 increases in astrocytes.

claim: Eleven-week-old mice were intraperitoneally injected with 100 μl of RML6 prions containing 8.02 log LD50 of infectious units per ml.
source: Eleven-week-old mice were intraperitoneally injected with 100 μl of RML6 prions (passage 6 of Rocky Mountain Laboratory strain mouse-adapted scrapie prions) containing 8.02 log LD50 of infectious units per ml.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Prion-inoculated mice allocated to the terminal group were sacrificed upon clear signs of terminal prion disease including piloerection, hind limb clasping, kyphosis and ataxia.
source: Prion-inoculated mice allocated to the terminal group were sacrificed upon clear signs of terminal PrD including piloerection, hind limb clasping, kyphosis and ataxia (corresponding to an age of 42 to 43 weeks).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and endpoint criteria used in the study.

claim: The terminal time point corresponds to the last time point when mice can be humanely euthanized and is reached 31–32 weeks post-intraperitoneal prion inoculation.
source: This time point corresponds to the last time point when mice can be humanely euthanized and is reached 31–32 weeks post -ntraperitoneal prion inoculation.
evidence: This describes the timing of the terminal endpoint in the experimental model.
